title: Custodian Lifeboat & Safety Channel — PRD draft
summary: Introduce a light-weight tenant protection mechanism (the "Custodian Lifeboat") and an operator-controllable Safety Channel to handle transient microbursts and noisy neighbors without global throttles. Goal: keep latency SLOs for high-priority tenants while providing economic burst capacity for lower-priority workloads.
body:
Context:
We have many draft designs for burst credits, warm pools, and lane-based autoscalers. Operators want a simple, auditable way to move tenants into a protected 'lifeboat' with constrained but latency-preserving execution during severe contention. Product wants a pattern that's easy to reason about, test, and expose to customers as a recoverable fallback option.

Problem statement:
- Microbursts and correlated demand across tenants produce tail latency spikes and make autoscaler tuning brittle.
- Full preemption or broad throttles cause cascading failures for moderate-priority workloads.
- Customers need transparent, SLA-safe degradation paths and an operator-friendly recovery channel.

Proposal (high level):
We define two cooperating constructs: 1) Custodian Lifeboat (CL): a per-tenant soft quarantine that isolates a tenant's compute to a constrained lane with strict latency budget, degraded throughput, and controlled fallback behaviors; 2) Safety Channel (SC): an operator- and policy-driven routing lane that can accept requests eligible for best-effort burst execution with bounded latency tail.

Key behaviors and rules:
- Triggering CL:
  - Automatic triggers: sustained 99.9th percentile latency above tenant SLO for 3x window, sustained error-rate increase, or collision with higher-priority tenant claim on the same pool.
  - Manual trigger: ops can move tenant to CL via console/CLI for incident isolation.
- CL runtime constraints:
  - CPU/GPU concurrency per tenant limited (configurable per tier).
  - Strict sequence-length caps and model fidelity fallback (quantized variant or smaller model family) to reduce per-token work.
  - KV cache warm-reuse disabled for large fanout patterns to avoid noisy cache pollution.
  - Burst allowance: a small fixed token budget per minute (e.g., 5% of normal tokens) to allow critical jobs to complete.
- Safety Channel semantics:
  - SC is an opportunistic routing lane (separate queue) with a tail-latency SLA (soft SLO) and a bounded retry/backoff policy.
  - Requests routed to SC are considered 'best-effort' and can be evicted if capacity needed for SLO-preserving lanes.
  - Customers may mark routes as SC-eligible using an attribute (e.g., route.meta.burst=best_effort).

APIs & UX:
- Console: one-click 'isolate tenant' (move to CL), with immediate estimate of throughput/latency impact and roll-back button.
- Route-level toggle: 'Allow best-effort Safety Channel' (on/off) with per-route cost/latency preview.
- CLI: redwoodctl tenant lifeboat enter|exit --reason ... --expected-duration ...

Policy matrix (examples):
- Tier A (enterprise SLA-critical): never auto-promoted to SC; CL only as last-resort manual isolation.
- Tier B (balanced): auto CL allowed after retries and can be routed to SC with low token caps.
- Tier C (developer/experimental): SC routing default true, larger burst window but lower priority eviction.

Autoscaler integration:
- Autoscaler will expose a 'protected_headroom' estimate representing capacity required to keep Tier A SLOs. If headroom crosses threshold, autoscaler starts preemptive migration of Tier C workloads to SC and reduces concurrency for CL tenants to reclaim headroom.
- Warm-pool interaction: CL tenants cannot consume warm-pool slots by default; warm-pool use can be allowed as a paid option (so customers pay to stay out of CL).

Observability and auditing:
- Per-request metadata tags for SC/CL routing and eviction reasons.
- Dashboards: per-tenant CL-days, SC-evictions, reclaimed-headroom minutes, and incident correlation view.
- Audit trail: who triggered manual CL, reason, and rollback history.

SLO & billing implications:
- Move to CL is a 'degradation' event. For Tier A customers we must reduce billing impact by offering credit or free warm-pool fallback. For other tiers, CL should be associated with a warning but no automatic crediting (configurable).
- Safety Channel requests billed at a discounted best-effort rate. Billing model needs ops/finance alignment.

Security and compliance notes:
- CL isolation must preserve tenant data boundaries; even in CL, data must not be exposed to other tenants.
- Logs and traces in CL remain full fidelity for debugging but access controls apply.

Implementation sketch (phases):
- Phase 0 (spike, 3 wks): implement SC queue + request metadata, simple eviction; console mockups.
- Phase 1 (MVP, 8 wks): CL toggle + basic runtime constraints (concurrency cap, model fallback), autoscaler hooks for protected_headroom.
- Phase 2 (8–12 wks): warm-pool policy adjustments, billing integration, per-tenant dashboards, manual rollback UX.
- Phase 3 (ongoing): simulation harness, chaos testing, multi-region policy refinement.

Success metrics (30/60/90):
- 30 days: SC routing engaged by at least 15% of medium-tier customers in test clusters; dashboards populated.
- 60 days: Measured 99.9th latency reduction for Tier A customers on contested pools by >35% during incidents.
- 90 days: Reduce operator manual evictions by 50% and capture clear billing policy for SC requests.

Open questions / trade-offs:
- How aggressive should the autoscaler be in migrating tenants vs reducing concurrency? Risk: oscillation.
- Billing sensitivity: how to price SC to avoid abuse but keep it economically attractive?
- Model fidelity fallbacks may cause unacceptable hallucination/regression for some customers—how to surface warnings and allow opt-out?

Operational runbook (short):
- Detection: alert when pool headroom <= protected_headroom threshold.
- Mitigation: trigger SC routing for eligible routes; if degradation persists escalate to manual CL for top noisy tenants.
- Recovery: diagnostics + gradual roll-back; maintain audit log of actions.

Next steps and owners:
- Product: finalize policy matrix and customer-visible UX (Sofia Ramirez) — 2 weeks.
- Eng infra: prototype SC queue + eviction (Ethan Walker) — spike 3 wks.
- Eng runtime: implement per-tenant caps + model fallback hook (Aisha Patel) — MVP 8 wks.
- Finance/Legal: proposal for SC billing and SLA language (Michael Chen) — 2 weeks.

Notes to reviewers:
- This draft favors operational simplicity and clear auditability over fully automatic credit economies. The intent is to reduce severity of noisy neighbor incidents quickly while giving customers control and visibility. Please call out missing edge-cases (multi-model pipelines, long-running stream sessions) and any regulatory concerns for CL data handling.
